forces.title: Persistent High Energy and Input Costs Burden European Producers
forces.description: European chemical producers face structurally higher energy prices compared to the US and China, exacerbated by the Iran war pushing up oil and gas costs. This increases production expenses, weighing heavily on margins, particularly for basic chemical companies. Additional LNG supply offers some relief, but sustainable cost reductions require substantial investment in renewable energy and hydrogen infrastructure. These elevated costs hinder global competitiveness and necessitate strategic shifts towards electrification and bio-based feedstocks.
forces.source_title: Temporary uptick for Dutch chemicals masks ongoing challenges

forces.title: Middle East Logistics Disruptions Limit Feedstock Availability and Increase Costs
forces.description: Geopolitical conflict in the Middle East, particularly around the Strait of Hormuz, has led to logistics disruptions and limited feedstock availability globally. This directly impacts European chemical producers, who, while less dependent on the Gulf region (around 20% of feedstock needs) than Asian counterparts, still face raw material volatility and increased transport costs. These disruptions contribute significantly to cost uncertainty and margin pressure, requiring companies to review supplier resilience and inventory planning to maintain production continuity.

forces.title: Global Overcapacity and Cheap Asian Imports Intensify Competition
forces.description: Global petrochemical production capacity has expanded by 65% over the past 15 years, with continued growth expected, particularly from China. This overcapacity, combined with an inflow of cheap, partly subsidized chemical imports from Asia and the artificially low value of the Chinese yuan, exerts significant pressure on European chemical producers. Upstream petrochemical and basic chemical segments are most acutely affected, leading to job cuts and plant closures. The large and increasing EU trade deficit in chemical products with China highlights the intensity of this competitive strain.
forces.source_title: Temporary uptick for Dutch chemicals masks ongoing challenges

forces.title: Growing Regulatory Burden and Administrative Complexity in Europe
forces.description: European chemical companies are grappling with increasing administrative complexity and regulatory burdens, which amplify existing challenges like high input costs. New EU regulations, such as the Packaging and Waste Regulation applying from August 2026 and restrictions on chemicals/heavy metals in food contact packaging, necessitate compliance investments. Furthermore, growing societal constraints on plastics and the phase-out of free emission allowances under the ETS for hard-to-abate products add to operational and financial pressures, making the operating environment in Europe increasingly challenging compared to other regions.
forces.source_title: A dual transformation agenda for Europe’s chemicals industry

forces.title: Weakening Demand from Key European Customer Industries
forces.description: Europe's broader economic downturn has significantly impacted major chemical customer industries, such as automotives, with production increasingly shifting away from Europe. This decline in demand from crucial end-markets directly translates into reduced orders and volume for chemical producers, contributing to a sustained imbalance between supply and demand. This trend, coupled with ongoing overcapacity in the chemicals sector, compresses margins and necessitates a re-evaluation of product lines and strategic investments to align with evolving market realities.
forces.source_title: A dual transformation agenda for Europe’s chemicals industry

forces.title: Declining European Chemical Capacity Utilization and Plant Closures
forces.description: The European Union's chemical capacity utilization has consistently been approximately seven percentage points below its long-term average of around 82 percent. This underutilization is a structural issue, compounded by a sixfold surge in announced chemical plant closures since 2022, resulting in a combined capacity loss of 37 million tonnes, or 9% of the region’s production capacity. This trend reflects fundamental market shifts and economic pressures, leading to asset devaluation and erosion of industrial ecosystems, making strategic repositioning and operational efficiency critical for survival.
forces.source_title: A dual transformation agenda for Europe’s chemicals industry

forces.title: AI and Semiconductor Boom Drives Demand for Electronic Chemicals
forces.description: The rapid acceleration of AI adoption and the expansion of its supporting infrastructure, including microchips, memory, and storage, are creating significant demand for specialized electronic chemicals and materials. These include photoresist, wet chemicals, and thermally conductive adhesives crucial for manufacturing and functioning of electronic devices. This market offers compelling growth opportunities, with several segments projected to see 5-10% CAGRs and EBITDA margins over 20% to 2030, presenting an attractive focus area for chemical companies to leverage existing capabilities and pursue M&A.
forces.source_title: Opportunities for Chemical Companies in the AI Infrastructure Boom

forces.title: Necessity for Dual Transformation to Rebuild Competitiveness
forces.description: European chemical companies face a critical imperative for 'dual transformation'—radically reshaping portfolios, assets, and industrial footprints for a structurally different market environment, while simultaneously generating sufficient cash and operational performance from existing businesses to fund this repositioning. This approach is essential to address lagging performance, intense global competition, and escalating input costs. Leaders must make difficult strategic choices, redefine industrial ecosystems, and build execution speed to ensure long-term competitiveness and avoid erosion of innovation capacity and supply chains.
forces.source_title: A dual transformation agenda for Europe’s chemicals industry

forces.title: Petrochemical Ecosystem Relies on Naphtha Cracking for Key Byproducts
forces.description: The broader petrochemical ecosystem depends on a diversified feedstock mix, with naphtha cracking playing a structural role beyond polyethylene (PE) production. Unlike ethane cracking, naphtha cracking produces essential byproducts like propylene, C-4 streams, and aromatics (benzene, toluene, xylenes) that are crucial inputs for materials such as rubbers, synthetic fibers, and engineering plastics. The anticipated decline in oil refining, driven by electrified transportation, could constrain naphtha supply, making these critical petrochemical byproducts more costly and complex to produce through alternative processes.

forces.title: Policy-Driven Demand for Sustainable Polyethylene Creates New Market Segments
forces.description: Policymakers in higher-cost regions like Europe are playing a more active role in shifting demand towards sustainable forms of polyethylene (PE). Demand mandates, such as recycled content requirements, create guaranteed demand for specific types of PE. Waste regulations, like restrictions on landfills or incineration, increase the supply and use of recycled plastics. Additionally, carbon-related measures, including carbon pricing and border adjustments, raise the cost of more emissions-intensive production. These policies create market segments where competition is based on sustainability or regulatory compliance rather than solely on cost, enabling domestic producers to compete on different terms.

forces.title: Temporary Stockpiling and Reduced Asian Competition Offer Brief Reprieve
forces.description: The Dutch chemical industry experienced a temporary uptick due to the initial closure of the Strait of Hormuz, which reduced foreign competition from Asian producers and triggered precautionary inventory building by customers. This eased demand for European chemical products, providing a brief period of production growth and fuller order books. However, this rebound is temporary; as trade flows normalize, the underlying structural challenges of overcapacity and cheap imports are expected to resurface, highlighting the cyclical nature of this relief.
forces.source_title: Temporary uptick for Dutch chemicals masks ongoing challenges

forces.title: Dutch Government Support Schemes Aim to Enhance Industry Competitiveness
forces.description: The Dutch government is actively implementing measures to level the playing field and support its chemical industry. The Indirect Cost Compensation scheme for large electricity consumers has been reintroduced for three years, aiming to dampen high electricity costs and narrow the gap with neighboring countries. Future policies include further reducing electricity costs for basic industry from 2028 and abolishing the national CO2 levy. These governmental interventions are designed to support a recovery in chemical plant utilization and improve the competitive position of Dutch producers against international rivals.
forces.source_title: Temporary uptick for Dutch chemicals masks ongoing challenges

forces.title: Rising CO2 Costs and ETS Rules Drive Greening Pressures
forces.description: European chemical producers face increasing pressure from rising CO2 costs and stringent ETS rules, necessitating significant investments in electrification and the adoption of bio-based feedstocks. While Brussels may offer some leeway, such as a slower phase-out of free emission allowances, the fundamental need for faster greening and reduced reliance on fossil fuels remains. This transformation, whether government-supported or not, is crucial for securing a future-proof competitive position but adds considerable operational and capital expenditure burdens, particularly for producers of hard-to-abate chemical products not covered by CBAM.
forces.source_title: Temporary uptick for Dutch chemicals masks ongoing challenges

forces.title: Geopolitical Tensions and Trade Fragmentation Increase Supply Chain Volatility
forces.description: Rising geopolitical tension, trade fragmentation, and localized disruptions are increasing volatility across materials supply chains, prompting a necessary redesign from efficiency optimization to resilience. The ongoing crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, for instance, significantly impacts feedstock and energy prices, as well as global shipping. This heightened uncertainty means customers increasingly expect supply continuity, short lead times, and greater flexibility. For chemical companies, navigating these risks requires strengthening supply chain management, diversifying sourcing, and maintaining robust liquidity buffers to absorb potential shocks.
forces.source_title: The next wave of value in the materials supply chain

viewpoints.title: Electronic Chemicals are a Compelling Growth Area Amidst AI Boom
viewpoints.description: Electronic chemicals and materials are emerging as a compelling focus for chemicals companies seeking growth, driven by accelerating AI demand. Several segments are projected to see 5-10% CAGRs to 2030 with EBITDA margins exceeding 20%. This opportunity spans microchips, thermal management, and robotics, presenting attractive returns despite a global industry downcycle. High R&D and long qualification cycles act as significant barriers to entry, encouraging sticky supplier-customer relationships and co-development, making this a strategic area for investment and M&A.
viewpoints.source_title: Opportunities for Chemical Companies in the AI Infrastructure Boom

viewpoints.title: Irish Chemicals Sector Faces Profitability Decline Due to High Costs and Disruptions
viewpoints.description: Profitability in the Irish chemicals sector is expected to decline, primarily due to high energy and input costs. Middle East logistics disruptions have limited feedstock availability globally, while volatility in oil-linked raw material prices creates cost uncertainty and margin pressure. The sector remains under moderate pressure, with near-term performance heavily dependent on the evolution of input costs, demand trends, and the broader macroeconomic environment. Operators need to prioritize margin protection, review pricing, and strengthen supplier resilience.

viewpoints.title: Dutch Chemicals Enjoy Temporary Relief But Structural Challenges Persist
viewpoints.description: The Dutch chemical industry experienced a temporary uplift in production and order books due to the Strait of Hormuz closure, which reduced Asian competition and encouraged stockpiling. However, this relief is temporary. Structural issues such as global overcapacity, cheap subsidized imports from Asia, and persistently high energy and CO2 costs in Europe will continue to pressure output once trade flows normalize. Upstream petrochemical and basic chemical producers are particularly vulnerable, necessitating strategic adjustments and greening efforts.
viewpoints.source_title: Temporary uptick for Dutch chemicals masks ongoing challenges

viewpoints.title: Europe's Chemicals Industry Requires Dual Transformation for Competitiveness
viewpoints.description: Europe's chemical industry is at a critical inflection point, with lagging performance and negative total shareholder returns. Structural challenges like higher input costs, intensified global competition from China, and a broader economic downturn affecting customer industries are amplified. Traditional incremental improvements are insufficient; companies must pursue a 'dual transformation'—radically repositioning portfolios and operations for a different market while simultaneously generating cash and improving performance from existing businesses. Failing to act now risks losing entire value chains and competitive standing.
viewpoints.source_title: A dual transformation agenda for Europe’s chemicals industry

viewpoints.title: European Polyethylene Production Faces Limited Investment Due to Cost and Regulation
viewpoints.description: European polyethylene (PE) production is seeing limited new investment, leading to a projected phase-out of up to five million tons of yearly ethylene capacity over the next five years. This reflects weaker feedstock competitiveness compared to ethane-advantaged regions, coupled with higher capital costs, longer and less predictable permitting timelines, and growing regulatory and societal constraints on plastics. Operators are increasingly opting to run downstream PE assets using imported ethylene rather than reinvesting in fully integrated crackers, signaling a shift towards more flexible production models.

demand_drivers.description: Accelerating demand for AI cascading into supporting infrastructure (microchips, memory, storage) and automation (robotics), requiring specialized electronic chemicals and materials like photoresist, wet chemicals, and thermally conductive adhesives.

demand_drivers.driver: Shift to advanced node technology in microchips
demand_drivers.description: Advanced microchip manufacturing requires more specialized materials, directly affecting yield, reliability, and performance across the value chain.
Growth in electronics manufacturing in Asia, the US, and the EU drives demand for electronic chemicals and materials.

market_sizing.methodology: Total addressable market for electronic chemicals and materials across the semiconductor supply chain. BCG estimates; AI and advanced computing represent important incremental growth drivers. Several sectors in this space are expected to see CAGRs of 5 to 10 percent to 2030.
market_sizing.source_title: Opportunities for Chemical Companies in the AI Infrastructure Boom

market_sizing.methodology: Global gross productive investment in the chemicals sector, averaged over 2022-2023 market exchange rates. China accounted for $158 billion, the United States for $135 billion, Japan and South Korea for $48 billion, and the EU-27 for $43 billion.

demand_drivers.description: PE demand is closely tied to population growth and urbanization, particularly in emerging economies.
PE is a foundational input in modern economies, widely used in packaging, construction, medical devices, and industrial products.

market_sizing.methodology: Global installed capacity for polyethylene (PE) production. Demand growth for PE is projected to rebound to approximately 3 percent annually, approaching 200 million tons annually by 2035.
